title: ESA Hera Mission Closes In on Asteroids After NASA DART Impact
byline: Сollin Rugg View all posts by Сollin Rugg
excerpt: ESA’s Hera mission approaches asteroids Didymos and Dimorphos to inspect the crater left by NASA’s DART crash, deploying CubeSats to assess planetary defence.
content:
The European Space Agency is closing in on deep space history as its Hera mission prepares to rendezvous with the binary asteroid system Didymos and Dimorphos, travelling at 12 kilometres per second relative to Earth. The probe will provide the first direct, high-resolution post-impact assessment of Dimorphos following NASA’s Double Asteroid Redirection Test (DART), which intentionally collided with the moonlet in 2022 to alter its trajectory.

Launched aboard a SpaceX Falcon-9 rocket from Cape Canaveral, Florida, on 7 October 2024, the spacecraft spent just over two years navigating across interplanetary space. Now standing as the first operational venture under the agency’s Space Safety Programme, the mission will begin acquiring baseline measurements of the binary pair from distances between 25 and 30 kilometres away.

The upcoming operations mark a crucial step forward for global planetary defence initiatives, transitioning planetary protection from speculative physics into precise, measurable science.

The Science Behind the Didymos-Dimorphos Binary System

The primary target of the expedition, the asteroid 65803 Didymos, was originally discovered by the Kitt Peak Spacewatch survey on 11 April 1996. Measuring 780 metres across, Didymos completes an orbit around the Sun every 2.1 years and rotates rapidly on its axis once every 2.2 hours. In 2003, astronomers detected its companion moonlet, Dimorphos, which measures 151 metres in diameter.

Much like Earth’s Moon, this binary pair features dark, silicon-rich material. Operating at 1.5 astronomical units from the Sun, the rendezvous takes place in a dim lighting environment, yet it generates sufficient solar exposure to power Hera’s two 5-metre solar arrays.

These rock piles are thought to be at their limits in terms of holding together versus flying apart.

Before its deliberate impact, DART confirmed that Dimorphos behaves as a structural “rubble pile,” structurally similar to asteroids Bennu and Ryugu, which were previously explored by NASA’s Osiris-REx and JAXA’s Hayabusa-2. DART’s 6.6-kilometre-per-second impact compressed the moonlet’s original 11-hour, 55-minute orbit by approximately 32 minutes, generating an extensive debris stream in surrounding space.

Planetary Defence: Misconceptions vs Factual Mechanics

Popular depictions often treat kinetic deflection as a simple ballistic push against a solid mountain of rock. In reality, scientists must account for the loose cohesion of rubble-pile asteroids, where impacts eject plumes that deliver additional recoil momentum back into the primary body.

Mission Attribute Specification Detail
Primary Spacecraft ESA Hera probe (Space Safety Programme)
Target Asteroid Pair 65803 Didymos (780 m) & Dimorphos (151 m)
Approach Speed 12 km/s relative to Earth
Operational Distance 25 to 30 km baseline survey
DART Impact Reduction Shortened orbital period by ~32 minutes
Secondary CubeSats Milani (Italy) & Juventas (Luxembourg)

Deploying Deep-Space CubeSats into Microgravity

To examine the altered planetary body without endangering the main bus, the spacecraft carries two miniaturised CubeSats engineered specifically for low-gravity environments. Standing on the boulder-strewn landscape of either asteroid would reveal a spinning sky dominated by its companion, where gravitational pull is so faint that an object would descend to the surface at a days-long, leisurely rate.

Shortly after arrival, Hera will deploy the secondary craft to execute targeted scientific assignments:

  • Milani: Built by Tyvak International in Turin, Italy, this probe will map spectral composition and investigate the dust environment surrounding both Didymos and Dimorphos.
  • Juventas: Developed by GomSpace in Luxembourg, this craft will probe internal structures using low-frequency radar and may eventually touch down directly onto Dimorphos.

Following the completion of its primary baseline survey through 2027, mission controllers may opt to repurpose the spacecraft as a long-term technology demonstrator to validate autonomous navigation techniques deep within the Solar System.

💡 The upcoming close-up reconnaissance will provide vital ground truth on how kinetic impacts reshape fragile asteroids.
